result:
Short version: it's an asymmetric, many-to-one mapping around the newline bytes, and that's by design in httpd's tables (`os_toascii` / `os_toebcdic`).

**ASCII 0x0A → EBCDIC 0x15.** The outbound table maps ASCII LF to EBCDIC `NL` (0x15), *not* the "true" EBCDIC LF at 0x25.

**Round-trip 0x15 → 0x0A: yes.** `os_toascii[0x15] == 0x0A`, so a byte you produced from an ASCII newline comes back as 0x0A cleanly. The 0x0A ↔ 0x15 pair is stable.

**EBCDIC 0x25 from elsewhere → also 0x0A, but it does *not* survive a round trip.** `os_toascii[0x25]` is likewise 0x0A, so an inbound 0x25 (a real EBCDIC LF from some other system) gets folded onto the same ASCII newline. But since ASCII 0x0A only ever maps back to 0x15, that 0x25 silently becomes 0x15 if it's ever converted back out. Two EBCDIC bytes (0x15 and 0x25) collapse onto one ASCII byte (0x0A), and the reverse direction only regenerates 0x15.

Practical implication: newlines that originate on your ASCII side are safe both ways. But if you're relaying EBCDIC text that used 0x25 as its line terminator, don't expect 0x25 to come out the far end — it'll have been normalized to 0x15. If preserving the original EBCDIC LF matters, you can't rely on httpd's translation layer to keep it distinct from NL.
